body.p: This study provided useful information regarding the role of a subpopulation of cortical interneurons (Chrna2-expressing Martinotti cells) in motor learning and cortical dynamics. However, while some behavior and imaging data are compelling, limitations in the motor-learning task design and data analysis make it difficult to support the central conclusions.
Summary:

In this manuscript, Malfatti et al. study the role of Chrna2 Martinotti cells (Mα2 cells), a subset of SST interneurons, for motor learning and motor cortex activity. The authors trained mice on a forelimb prehension task while recording neuronal activity of pyramidal cells using calcium imaging with a head-mounted miniscope. While chemogenetically increasing Mα2 cell activity did not affect motor learning, it changed pyramidal cell activity such that activity peaks become sharper and differently timed than in control mice. Moreover, co-active neuronal assemblies become more stable with a smaller spatial distribution. Increasing Mα2 cell activity in previously trained mice did increase performance on the prehension task and led to increased theta and gamma band activity in the motor cortex. On the other hand, genetic ablation of Mα2 cells affected fine motor movements on a pasta handling task while not affecting the prehension task. While overall this study addresses an important and timely question, limitations in the design of the motor learning task and data analysis significantly weaken the conclusions drawn in this manuscript.
Strengths:

The proposed question of how Chrna2-expressing SST interneurons affect motor learning and motor cortex activity is important and timely. The study employs sophisticated approaches to record neuronal activity and manipulate the activity of a specific neuronal population in behaving mice over the course of motor learning. The authors analyze a variety of neuronal activity parameters, comparing different behavior trials, stages of learning, and the effects of Mα2 cell activation. The analysis of neuronal assembly activity and stability over the course of learning by tracking individual neurons throughout the imaging sessions is notable, since technically challenging, and yielded the interesting result that neuronal assemblies are more stable when activating Mα2 cells.
Overall, the study provides compelling evidence that Mα2 cells regulate certain aspects of motor behaviors, likely by shaping circuit activity in the motor cortex.
Weaknesses:

I appreciate the authors' efforts to address the remaining issues raised by the reviewers and agree that it becomes clearer by refocusing the study away from learning towards effects of Ma2 cell activation on motor execution. I also appreciate added clarifications throughout the manuscript.

That said the study still relies heavily on measuring changes throughout "performance refinement", which is just another word for learning. Given their task design, it is hard to assess any learning or refinement over the course of training. This makes it hard to interpret why certain changes in neuronal activity occur at the defined sessions. The main conclusion thus is that there is "a complex interplay between Mα2 activity, oscillatory brain dynamics, and motor function", as the authors state as well in their discussion. I would encourage a further focus or restriction of the data presentation and interpretation on motor execution and limit any plasticity findings on training session 6, where the reaching task properly starts, such as in the study the authors reference (10.1016/j.neuron.2021.07.030).

Relatedly, the authors cannot say that "enhancing Mα2 cell excitability improved the performance of a motor task relying on an already refined skill (Figure 6C)" (lines 1134-1136). Since there is no improvement in success ratio throughout the training prior to CLZ injection (Supp Fig. 7A), there is no evidence for learning or skill refinement in the period where the pellet is presented on the plate.

Regarding the Ca2+ image analysis, the baseline subtraction approach the authors use only appropriately reduces part of the technical variations seen with 1p Ca2+ imaging. It only partially accounts for differences in GCaMP expression or different illumination across cells, or slower task-independent fluctuations in neuronal activity. Given the goal of the analysis is to show activity modulation in the peri-trial interval around prehension onset, some version of trial-wise baseline normalization (which is commonly used) is necessary and would likely result in less confusing results.
Minor:
- Unclear which session traces in figure 1I are from.
- Label in Supp Fig. 7A should say "switch from spoon to plate".
The following is the authors’ response to the previous reviews.

disp-quote.p: This valuable study addresses a critical question regarding the role of a subpopulation of cortical interneurons (Chrna2-expressing Martinotti cells) in motor learning and cortical dynamics. However, despite the inclusion of interesting behavioral and imaging data, significant limitations remain, even after revision, in the design of the motor learning task and the associated data analyses. As a result, the presented data are incomplete to support the central conclusions.

body.p: We appreciate the valuable feedback. To address these concerns, we have rephrased all conclusions to explicitly focus on motor execution consolidation rather than learning, as our task design inherently emphasizes performance refinement over acquisition. This reframing is now fully supported by compelling evidence from our data and analysis, demonstrating that Mα2 cell activation reduces pyramidal cell population plasticity and improves motor execution.

disp-quote.p: In line 331, the authors refer to session 5 as “training,” describing it as the final spoon session, and session 6 as “re-training,” because it is the first session in which the pellet is presented on the plate rather than on the spoon. However, in Fig. 1F-H, even in the Ctrl group, it is clear that the performance drops significantly in session 5, which is supposed to be the easiest session before switching to the more difficult plate condition.

body.p: As described in the methods, the task is made progressively harder (as evidenced by the success ratio curve), therefore a lower performance in session 5 (the hardest spoon session) is expected, as now explicitly stated in the results (lines 816-825).

disp-quote.p: In the classic pellet-reaching task, the spoon sessions would typically be considered “shaping”, while the plate sessions would represent the actual training phase. However, in this manuscript, the authors still insist on referring to session 2 as “learning” and session 5 as “training.” I don’t understand the difference between session 2 and session 5, especially when session 5’s performance is lower than session 2 (even in Fig 1H when you compare succ ratio).

body.p: The experiments were designed to investigate the effect of Ma2 cell activation on learning and training outcomes. As we wanted to compare completely naive mice with mice that had been trained and that had learned the task, we included the first sessions with the spoon in our analysis. In many other studies or experimental set-ups those sessions would have been considered shaping. The reason for this design is that we did not want to miss early changes related to training and learning that could have a great impact on the final outcome, as most dendritic spines that correlate with learning are formed after the initial training session and are maintained in the second training session (10.1016/j.neuron.2021.07.030). During pilot studies, several different strategies were tested and it was discovered that the mice needed to succeed several times in the initial sessions in order to keep trying. Hence, the pellet presentation needed to be less challenging in the beginning than in the final sessions in which the pellet was presented on the plate. Therefore, as explained above, the task was made progressively harder throughout the session and from session to session, thus mice expectedly had more difficulty in session 5. We agree that the session names could be misleading, particularly in the context of our task design, and therefore changed all session labels to session numbers.

disp-quote.p: Since session 6 (on the plate) is considered as “retraining,” why don’t the authors present the behavioral results beyond session 6? As a result, it remains unclear whether the animals improved their performance during the retraining phase.

body.p: We agree, and now show behavior performance from sessions 1 to 10 for the behavioural group. Mice displayed a clear improvement after session 6, reaching a plateau after session 7 (Figure 1F-H). Unfortunately, due to technical challenges with reattaching the miniscope multiple times and following the same neurons over time, we do not have miniscope data from beyond session 6, which is why we initially only presented behavioural data up to session 6.

disp-quote.p: Lastly, in Fig. 4B the authors present only the success ratio and claim that performance improves with CLZ application. However, when comparing sessions 8-10 between the Ctrl and Cre+ groups, there already appears to be a baseline difference. CLZ treatment in Cre+ mice seem to bring performance only to the WT level rather than producing a clear improvement beyond baseline.

body.p: In the previous version (first submitted), we showed the success rate (number of success per minute), to the same conclusion. Note that our conclusion is supported by the effect of treatment found in Cre+, meaning that Cre+ improved upon CLZ (Ma2 cells increase in excitability) compared to NaCl (No change in Ma2 cell excitability). The control group is a control for the Ma2 cell activation specificity, and as expected it shows no treatment effect (since there is no hM3Dq expression, as already reported, Supplemental Table 1L). Further, the reviewer’s suggestion of a baseline difference between groups is not supported by our data, since no statistical differences were found on these comparisons (t-test eff. size < -1.587; p > 0.293; as already stated in the methods, the absence of significance bars “for any comparison means no significant difference was found”).

disp-quote.p: Regarding the alignment between imaging and behavior, the authors report ~100 prehensions per minute. However, the calcium imaging traces show fewer than 20-30 spikes over 150 seconds (~2.5 min; Fig. 1E). This discrepancy raises concerns about whether the authors can truly isolate calcium signals corresponding to individual prehension events (either successful ones or multiple combined events for unsuccessful attempts). The manuscript still does not present behavioral data that directly aligns prehension events with calcium imaging activity. Although the authors performed analyses suggesting that prehension-related activity does not systematically alter nonprehension epochs, this claim is difficult to evaluate without seeing the underlying traces. It is therefore unclear how the authors selected the example calcium traces aligned to prehension onset, given that there are more than 100 prehension events per minute.

body.p: If we understand this comment correctly, the reviewer presumes that there should be a direct relationship between upper motor neuron activity and prehension activity (i.e. muscle activity). Such one-to-one correspondence between prehension events and calcium transients in individual pyramidal neurons should not be expected.

Upper motor neurons do not fire in a direct, event-by-event relationship with movements. Instead, motor actions emerge from distributed population activity, where individual neurons contribute sparsely and variably. Classical work described in the book Corticospinal function and voluntary movement by Porter and Lemon (1993) show that the relationship between single-neuron firing and muscle contraction is indirect and probabilistic. This circumstance required spike-triggered averaging based on several thousands of recordings to reveal consistent relationships between neuronal firing and motor output, precisely because individual spikes are neither necessary nor sufficient for a movement instance.

Calcium imaging accentuates this dissociation. Calcium signals are a temporally filtered and nonlinear proxy of spiking activity, with limited sensitivity to single spikes and a bias toward burst-like or temporally clustered firing. As a result, many individual action potentials, especially those occurring in isolation, may not generate detectable calcium transients. Therefore, observing fewer calcium events than behavioral actions is expected and does not imply a failure to capture relevant neural dynamics.

Thus, motor cortex representations during skilled behaviors such as prehension are distributed across neuronal ensembles rather than encoded at the level of single neurons. Each prehension recruits a subset of neurons, and each neuron contributes only intermittently across trials. Consequently, the appropriate level of analysis is not event-by-event alignment for individual cells, but rather population-level dynamics (e.g., ensemble activity patterns, dimensionality reduction, or trial-averaged responses aligned to behavior).

We have not selected “example calcium traces aligned to prehension onset”. We performed all quantifications on the average of all trials, and we thus show one example of such traces in Figure I and all average traces in Supplemental Figure 3I. All trials were included, therefore there is no “selection”, as already explained in the methods section (lines 607-611).

Taken together, the apparent discrepancy between behavioral event rate and calcium event frequency reflects known principles of motor cortex coding and calcium imaging limitations, rather than a methodological inconsistency. This explanation is now added to the discussion section (lines 1186-1211).

Regarding the baseline effect analysis (Supplemental Figure 3I), we do not understand the claim that the underlying traces for the quantification shown cannot be seen, when they are explicitly shown in the same figure (Supplemental Figure 3A-E). We agree that the figure legends for Supplemental Figures 2 and 3 were missing the description of the traces shown as average traces of all trials for all neurons, with the shade showing the standard error of the mean. We now added this information to the Supplemental Figures 2 and 3 legends.

disp-quote.p: In Fig. 1I, the authors also did not address why neural activity during successful trials is already lower one second before movement onset. The longer traces provided do not help to explain this observation or clarify the origin of this pre-movement reduction in activity. It actually further suggests that there may be some artifacts in the imaging that could affect the analysis.

body.p: We understand that the example shown in Figure 1I can cause confusion, therefore we chose a clearer example neuron. As explained in the previous comment, no quantifications were made at the trial level, therefore Figure 1I shows the average +SEM of all trials.

disp-quote.p: Overall, because it remains difficult to understand exactly what the authors are analyzing (and because the definitions of the motor learning stages appear arbitrary) it is difficult to agree with the authors’ conclusion that Ma2s cells reduce PyrN cell assembly plasticity during learning, thereby possibly facilitating already acquired motor skills.

body.p: We rewrote our conclusions to better fit our results and thoroughly explained the calcium imaging analysis concerns above. No quantifications (nor claims) were done at single-level trial, and we clearly show the exact traces from where the quantifications were derived (Figure 1E, 1I; Supplemental Figure 2A-H and 3A-H.

disp-quote.p: While the authors addressed some of the concerns raised by the reviewers, several major limitations still exist in the revised manuscript.

(1) I appreciate the authors now showing more measures of the prehension task (total reaches, success reaches/min, and success ratio) and providing more details on the task design. However, it is unclear why the authors chose a task design that is somewhat different from the commonly used approach. Here they increase the distance of the food pellet each session and are thus making the task increasingly harder, whereas commonly the target distance is kept stable (See 10.1038/nature08389 for example). The result is that important readouts of learning (e. g. success rate) thus remain stable, making it impossible to judge if learning has occurred, without a control group of non-trained mice. This makes it impossible to judge if the task is affected by increased Ma2 cell excitability, since there is no reference of how these measurements are supposed to change in a mouse that learns or doesn’t learn the task.

During pilot studies, several different strategies were tested and it was discovered that the mice needed to succeed several times in the initial sessions in order to keep trying. Hence, the pellet presentation needed to be less challenging in the beginning than in the final sessions in which the pellet was presented on the plate. On previous pilot experiments, when the spoon distance was kept stable across sessions, most animals did not perform the task upon switching to the plate position (a large and abrupt increase in difficulty), whereas progressively increasing the difficulty led to more mice reaching for the plate target. We agree that this task design better reflects motor execution than learning, and have stated throughout the manuscript that learning is unaffected. We also reframed conclusions about learned motor execution to better fit our task design.

disp-quote.p: (2) Regarding the analysis of the calcium imaging data, it is still unclear why the authors cannot report a commonly used dF/F0 or z-score value, as recommended by both reviewers. The authors state the 1 sec time window prior to the prehension cannot be used as a baseline (F0), as there might be preparatory motor activity. In that case an even earlier window (such as -2 to -1sec) or z-scores should be used. The current version relabeling the background subtracted fluorescence signal as dF/F0 is misleading. Relatedly, it is unclear why the authors don’t think the 1 sec window before prehension cannot be used as baseline, but at the same time use the difference in calcium activity before and after prehension onset as a cut-off criterion for defining cells as modulated during prehension and including in the analysis.

body.p: As explained in the previous review round, we performed baseline subtraction as described in the methods section: "The baseline components were estimated using a running 8th percentile derived from kernel density estimation over a 250-frame window, and subtracted from each respective trace. Although true F0 estimation is not possible on 1-photon data, the baseline-subtracted trace is here referred to as ΔF/F. The fact that the label ΔF/F is commonly used in 1-photon data is misleading, since studies analyzing miniscope data using the label ΔF/F define F0 as the raw video frame minimum (e.g., 10.1371/journal.pbio.3000584, 10.1111/ejn.70190), mean of “non-spiking” periods for all neurons (e.g., 10.1016/j.crmeth.2025.101221), or providing no F0 definition (e.g., 10.1002/adfm.202511627, 10.3389/fnagi.2025.1550673, 10.1016/j.bpsgos.2025.100531, 10.1038/s41586-025-10096-w), none of which are true F0. We reiterate, as in the previous review round, that any use of the label ΔF/F is technically incorrect, not only here but in any study using 1-photon data.

After the previous review round we defined F0 as the baseline components estimated as described above, which is a much more reliable and standardized measure of baseline components estimation compared to the measures cited above, using an extensively validated algorithm (10.7554/eLife.38173), and labeled our data as ΔF/F since they are already properly scaled, as previously done (10.3389/fnagi.2025.1550673). However, after this discussion, we suggest reverting back to the more correct technical term “ΔF detr.”. This also aligns with previous other similar work (e.g., 10.1073/pnas.2503139122, 10.3389/fnsys.2026.1765204), and that is what our traces (and any traces from any study derived from 1-photon data) actually are.

We searched and found some studies analysing miniscope data that have z-scored fluorescence traces, but none of those provided a clear justification for doing so (e.g., 10.1016/j.isci.2026.115514, 10.1016/j.neuron.2025.07.020). We do not think that z-scoring appropriately scales fluorescence traces, particularly when baseline components are already subtracted. Fluorescence traces exhibit strong positive skewness, characteristic of calcium imaging data where the baseline is stable (after removing baseline components as described above) but transient events create a heavy tail, and z-scoring relies on the mean and standard deviation. In highly skewed distributions, both the mean and standard deviation are strongly influenced by the magnitude and frequency of these transients. Consequently, z-scoring the traces artificially compresses the baseline and distorts the relative amplitude of events, leading to biased comparisons between different cells by penalizing cells according to their own activity (more active cells will have more transients, therefore larger mean, and lower z-scored traces), instead of normalizing to a biologically meaningful scale. This can be easily demonstrated, take for example the signal fragment in Author response image 1.

caption.title: The A panel shows a fluorescence trace from one neuron.
caption.p: If we slice this trace in half (B), the background component is the same, since they are derived from the same cell. If we z-score those halves, the half with higher activity is penalized (C, blue), while the less active half is artificially increased (C, orange). Since both signals are from the same cell, if z-scoring the traces was an appropriate normalization procedure, the differences between them should remain, which is not the case. Therefore, it is clear that z-scoring does not properly scale fluorescence traces for the purpose of comparisons between cells.

body.p: Regarding the inclusion criterion, we used the difference between before and after activity precisely to include only neurons related to the task, which does not mean that the "before" epoch is baseline, only that it is not the same as the "after" epoch, as shown by data already included in the manuscript. Further, we already ran the suggested analysis (after/before ratio) and presented the full results set: “We found a three-way interaction effect of genotype, session, and prehension accuracy (Supplemental Table 2K; Supplemental Figure 4), with genotype effects for both accuracies on the naive session and successful prehensions during the learning session (Supplemental Table 2L-N), and accuracy effects in control mice across the learning and training sessions (Supplemental Table 2O-P). This indicates that Mα2 cell activity might selectively refine the neural signal balance during planning/execution phases of motor execution particularly on initial training sessions.”

disp-quote.p: (3) While the authors have improved their statistical reporting, key information is still missing in several places. For example, no N-numbers are listed in legends for figure 3, and there is no mention of the number of mice for analysis in figures 2 and 3. For clarity, the authors should also include the statistical test performed in the figure legends for any p-values shown in the figure.
